subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS2 Computing (variables, repetition and selection, designing and debugging programs); Scratch game-making sequence adapted from the school's Drive Scratch Game Maker resources (Y7-Y9 computing overview)

lessons.title: Variables: boxes that store information
objectives: Explain that a variable stores a value which can change
Use 'set' and 'change by' to update a variable
Trace the value of a variable through a short algorithm

keywords.def: a named box that stores a value which can change
the information stored in a variable
give a variable a starting value
add to or take away from a variable

starter: Bismillah. Say what an if-then-else does.
A game shows 'Score: 0'. Where does the computer remember the score?

teach.heading: A variable is a labelled box
bullets: The label is the name: score.
The value can change; the name stays.
teach.note: Use real boxes or a drawn box with a sticky note. Write score on the label and 0 inside. Change the number inside. Ask what stayed the same and what changed. Misconception: pupils think a variable name and its value are the same thing.

teach.heading: Set and change
teach.note: Act it out: pupils hold a whiteboard with the variable name and a number; you give instructions and they update. Ask: after set score to 0, change by 3, change by 2, what is score? (5).

teach.heading: Trace it
teach.note: Show a trace table with a column per line of the algorithm and a row for the value. Teach pupils to fill it in line by line. This is the foundation for trace tables later in secondary computing.

teach.heading: Variables in real life
teach.note: Ask pupils to give their own examples of something that changes and a computer must remember. Example: the number of steps counted by a fitness watch.

practice: set score to 5, change score by 3, change score by -2. What is score? (6)
set lives to 3, change lives by -1 twice. What is lives? (1)
What is the variable name and what is the value in: set coins to 10?
independent: Complete 4 trace tables for algorithms with 'set' and 'change' blocks.
Write an algorithm to keep score in a game where you earn 10 points for a star and lose 5 for a rock.
Design a variable box diagram for a game: choose 3 variables, name them and give each a starting value.
exit: set x to 4, change x by 6. What is x?
lessons.homework: Find two places on a device or game where a number changes. Name the variable and describe when it changes.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use physical boxes and counters; give a template trace table. Stretch: trace an algorithm containing a repeat loop that changes a variable each time.

lessons.title: Variables in Scratch: score and lives
objectives: Use set and change blocks to update a score
Show a variable on the stage and test it

keywords.def: the button in Scratch that creates a new variable
makes the variable's value visible on the stage
a variable that all sprites can use

starter: Bismillah. set score to 2, change score by 5. What is score?
What stays the same in a variable: the name or the value?
Why might a game need a lives variable?

teach.heading: Make a variable
bullets: Name it score; choose 'For all sprites'.
teach.note: Share the screen and make the variable step by step. Pupils follow on their own machines. Explain that a name like score tells us what the variable is for, so choose names that make sense.

teach.heading: Start at zero
teach.note: Show what happens if you forget to set score to 0: the score continues from last time. Misconception: pupils think Scratch resets variables automatically; it does not.

teach.heading: Change the score
teach.note: Build a clicker game: click the star sprite to add 1 to the score. Run it and click five times. Ask for predictions: what will the score be after 10 clicks? Check.

teach.heading: Lives and sensing
bullets: If touching the rock: change lives by -1.
teach.note: Preview the selection with variables. Do not build all of it now. Ask pupils what blocks they will need and in what order. Connect to selection from Year 4.

practice: Which block puts the score back to 0 at the start of the game?
What happens to the score if the sprite is clicked 7 times and each click changes score by 2? (14)
Name two good variable names for a game and say what each is for.
independent: Build a click game: a sprite appears at a random place and each click adds 1 to score.
Add a second variable called 'clicks' that counts every click even when the sprite is missed.
Test the game and write what the score and clicks are after you click 10 times.
exit: Why do we set the score to 0 when the green flag is clicked?
Which block changes a variable by adding a number?
lessons.homework: Improve the click game at home: make the sprite move to a new place each time it is clicked, and send a screenshot.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a half-built project with the variable already created and the blocks to arrange. Stretch: make each click worth 2 points and the score show on the stage in a large font.

lessons.title: Loops and conditions: forever, if and repeat until
objectives: Use 'forever' with 'if' to keep checking something
Use 'repeat until' to repeat until a condition is true
Explain the difference between a count-controlled and a condition-controlled loop

keywords.def: a loop which never stops until the program ends
a loop which stops when its condition becomes true
a sensing block that checks if sprites meet

starter: Bismillah. How do you make a sprite move 10 steps five times without writing the block five times?
set coins to 3, change coins by 2. What is coins?
What does an if block need before it can decide?

teach.heading: Counting loops
teach.note: Recap repeat from Year 3 with a quick square. Ask pupils how they would know how many times to repeat if they did not know the number in advance.

teach.heading: Repeat until
bullets: The loop stops when the condition is true.
We do not need to know how many.
teach.note: Demonstrate a sprite moving 5 steps repeat until touching the edge. Change the starting position and show the loop still works. Misconception: pupils think the loop stops immediately when the condition is first checked; it checks every time round.

teach.heading: Forever and if
bullets: if touching star: change score by 1.
teach.note: Build a catch game: a basket sprite moves with the arrow keys; inside a forever loop an if block checks touching star. Explain that a loop with a condition inside is how games check what is happening. Show what happens without the forever loop (the check only happens once).

teach.heading: Choosing the right loop
bullets: Know when to stop: repeat until.
teach.note: Give three scenarios and ask which loop fits: draw a hexagon, walk until you reach the wall, keep checking for key presses. Take answers using thumbs signals.

practice: Which loop would you use to make a sprite walk until it touches a wall?
Which loop would you use to draw a pentagon (5 sides)?
A game must always check if the player touches an enemy. Which loop? (forever)
independent: Build a sprite which moves across the stage until it touches the edge, then says 'Done!'.
Build a catch game where the basket moves left and right and score increases when it touches the falling star.
Test the game and debug any problems; write one change you made.
exit: Which loop stops only when a condition becomes true?
Why does the 'if touching' block need to be inside a forever loop?
lessons.homework: Think of a game you play. Write which actions would need a forever loop and which would need repeat.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a screenshot of the finished script to compare with theirs and label the loops with colour. Stretch: make the falling star start at a random place at the top each time.

lessons.title: Project: design, build and test a catching game
objectives: Design a game using a plan with sprites, variables and rules
Use variables, loops and selection together
Test, evaluate and improve the game

keywords.def: plan what your program will do
decide how well something works and how to improve it
what happens when something occurs in the game

starter: Bismillah. Name the three kinds of loop block we have used.
What should a game do when lives reach 0?

teach.heading: Design first
bullets: Who or what is the player?
What do you catch or avoid?
What are the variables and rules?
teach.note: Show a design template: sprites, variables, rules, extras. Model filling it in for a fruit-catching game with dates. Explain why designers plan before building. Tidy and careful work is part of excellence (ihsan).

teach.heading: Build in steps
teach.note: Decompose the project into steps (callback to Year 3) and display them. Pupils should test after each step. Encourage them to save their project often.

teach.heading: Test with a checklist
bullets: Does the score go up when caught?
Does the game end at 0 lives?
teach.note: Give a checklist to tick off. Explain that a good tester tries unexpected things too, such as holding two keys. Typical bug: the score keeps rising while the item is touching the player; fix with a move-back or hide.

teach.heading: Evaluate
bullets: Ask a friend to play your game.
teach.note: Teach evaluation sentences: 'My game works well because... To improve it I would...'. Encourage honest and gentle peer feedback. Give a few minutes for pupils to play each other's games via shared links.

practice: Design on screen: choose three variables for the game (score, lives, time) and give each a starting value.
Write the rule for losing a life in the form IF ___ THEN ___.
Plan three steps for building the game in the order you would do them.
independent: Complete the design template for your own catching game.
Build and test your game with at least one variable, one loop and one if block.
Fill in the evaluation: two things that work and one improvement.
exit: Name one variable in your game and say what it does.
What is one bug you fixed and how did you find it?
lessons.homework: Add one improvement to your game (a new level, a timer, or sounds) and write one sentence about how it changes the game.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a starter project with sprites and backdrop; give sentence starters for the design and evaluation. Stretch: add a second type of falling object that takes points away.
